newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban wins Saudi recognition, march blocked.
newsitem.headline: Taleban wins Saudi recognition, march blocked.

text.p: Afghanistan's Telaban militia decreed Islamic restrictions in the newly captured north on Monday and won Saudi recognition of its government, but opposition shelling blocked its march across a key pass.

The purist militia, bent on spreading its strict Islamic rule across Afghanistan, announced restrictions on men and women in the main northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif in line with those imposed earlier in Kabul and other Taleban-controlled areas.
Saudi Arabia on Monday became the second country after Pakistan to recognise the Taleban government in Afghanistan, and some diplomats said Gulf Arab neighbours were expected to follow Riyadh's move.

On the battle-front, a planned Taleban advance from Kabul to the north from the strategic Salang Pass was blocked by opposition shelling, but the militia said its forces were poised to take the northeastern province of Takhar.

In Mazar-i-Sharif, an announcer at a rally read out four new rules, decreeing that people should reopen their shops, women should wear the all-enveloping Burqa robe and stop working outside their homes and girls should stop going to school or university.

Later in the day, the Taleban broadcast further rules over mosque loudspeakers, banning music, telling women to stay at home unless accompanied by their husbands or first male relatives and ordering men to grow beards.
Witnesses said Taleban fighters raided the television in Mazar-i-Sharif, hurling video-cassettes against walls and ripping out ribbons of video-tapes.
Television repair shops emptied their display windows. Video rental shops hastily hid their stocks. Some residents buried their satellite dishes to prevent the Taleban from destroying them.

The fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, the opposition's main point of supply as well as their political capital, dealt a severe blow to the opposition. They now control less than 10 per cent of the country and are confined to mountainous territory in the northeast and centre of Afghanistan.

General Abdul Malik, who joined forces with the Taleban after staging a mutiny against opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum a week ago, announced that Islamic Sharia law would be applied in the north.
Girls and women would be excluded from schools and universities until there was enough money to build segregated facilities, he said.

Shelling overnight and on Monday by followers of guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood held up the Taleban advance through the Salang Pass, Afghanistan's north-south gateway north of the capital Kabul, despite a deal with a local pro-Masood commander, witnesses said.
Retreating opposition fighters had also blown up a bridge to slow the Taleban down.
The deal to hand over the Salang came a day after forces allied to the Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif in the north of Afghanistan, the opposition's capital.

Remaining opposition forces are being squeezed by Taleban forces moving south from Mazar-i-Sharif and north from Kabul. Masood, the chief military commander of the government ousted from Kabul by the Taleban last September, is holding out in the Panjsher valley close to the Salang Pass.

If the Salang falls, as the Taleban expect, it will cut the last link between Masood and Hezb-i-Wahadat, a mainly Shi'ite faction still fighting to retain control of central Afghanistan's Bamiyan province.
